blocks.x: Well let's start in on this is the first reel we're making today.
Yeah.
And what's your name?
My name's Thomas Allardy.
What do they call you?
Kid Thomas.
What do they call you?
Many names laughing.
Yeah, but what's your real name?
Mike Catherman.
Is that all? That's all. No more. You're not even Michael, huh?
At times, yeah. Usually Mike.
Yeah. No middle name?
No middle name.
What about you? You got a middle name?
Well my name is Dick Allen and I won't tell you my real name. I've heard of him.
Did you ever know kid Louis Armstrong Thomas?
No, I never met him.
You never met him?

I met him, but I never knowed him before, you know what I mean? When did he? Until he came here. He came, you know, when he went off and came back to the play. He played over there in Old River. And I saw him twice.
Was that the, uh...
Once at the auditorium.
Mm-hmm.
And once at the Gypsy Tea Room.
Oh, he came to the Gypsy Tea Room, huh?
Mm-hmm. Yeah. Mm-hmm.
What year was that?
Mm-hmm. Man, that must have been, it must have been around, way around, all the days or something. Mm-hmm.

Before World War II? Mm-hmm. I'll be doing time, I'll be doing time of the war. During the time of the war. I see. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. When you studied trumpet, by the way, what kind of method did you use?

I didn't have no method when I first started. Mm-hmm. No, you see I started, I started my, just myself, you know, just, you know, pick up the horn and play, you know. Well, first I started playing on, on trombone. Mm-hmm. First, I was on the key trombone, the valve. Mm-hmm. Then after that, I took the trumpet and different things, sliding trombone, tried that. Then I went back to the trumpet and I just stayed on the trumpet.
You liked that first?

Yeah, I liked the trumpet. So after I played the trumpet, then I began to, you know, make scales and practice until I was able to play a number, you know, so, you know what I mean, one number at the time, you know what I mean. Just stay on that one number, just keep playing, keep playing that one number. So after I got that number down really good, then I tried another number, see. Well, eventually, well, I had about three good numbers, you see. So then after we, after I tried the three number, I had three numbers down good. What I did, what we did, then we had a little band, see. So fella, he had a club and we had trumpet, drum, a bass, and a clarinet.
And something else we had, a banjo.

Yeah, we couldn't play no more than three numbers. We played it all night, over and over. Played slow once, then fast the next time, that's what I mean. So the fact that people liked it, you know, them days, they liked it, you know, there was no body kicker, but nothing like that, you know, it was satisfied, you know what I mean. So, well, after that, well, we went on and continued. We never stopped.
Tell him who was in the band, he'd like to know.
Oh yeah, well, Edmund, Edmund Hall, Robert, Robert Hall, he was the first one to stay with us.
Played what?
Clownet.
What did Edmund play?

He played Clownet too. See, he learned to Clownet. See, he left and he came down here, after our band began to get real, you know, good then, see, but Edmund, he took up Clownet, so Clowns, he played the banjo. He played the banjo, so another boy, he dead now, he was playing the bass. I forgot his name, I think I place his name now, but anyhow, we had.
You have a drummer, you say?
Yeah, we have a drummer, yeah. Who was he? Wallace.
Wallace, you don't know his last name?
No, that's all I know.
Wallace, I see. What kind of club was that you played for?

It was a, it was a, it was a, it was a, it was a, a ballroom, a ballroom downstairs, and a dance hall upstairs, you see? Whose place was it? It's in reserve, it's, it belongs to, uh, old man Moran. Moran. Uh-huh, yeah.
And is it still there? Yeah, the club's still there. I'd like to get a picture of you in front of it somehow. Yeah, it's still there, mm-hmm.
That'd be nice to have.
You see on that side, they had a, they had a, they had a, they had a, they had a, they

had a dance hall, you see? After, after that, one of the brothers had the club, you see? The ballroom, and plays up there. Other brother, he built a dance hall, a pavilion, you see? That's a nice place of pavilion. We used to play that, we started playing that. See? for the band, you see? Then after that, after that, he, after our band got real good, then the man, we didn't have no name for the band, you see? So his, his brother-in-law was a druggist, you see? Got a drug store, have a drug store. So he, he had put up a medicine, and he named the band after the medicine. I see. Yeah, Niles band, see? It was a Niles band, that's why I was named for our band. Uh-huh. See? All right, so, well, we just went on and went on and keep, kept, kept playing.
But you had to have a teacher sometime to know as much as you know.

No, we ain't had no, I'm gonna tell you, I'm gonna come, I'm gonna come to that. Okay. See? Well, we went on. We went on like that for a long time. So when Edmund, Robert, he left. All right. Edmund, my cousin, you see, they had another drummer with my cousin, 9L Thomas, you see? Well, he, he, he was playing drums, he was a small kid, he was playing in, in one of the musical bands, all, all musicals, you see? Well, he used to have a teacher to come out there and teach them fellas, you see? Yeah. So when he, when he's playing with us, so he left, he went to Baton Rouge. All right. Edmund left. See? All right. Clarence left. That left me. I'm the only, last one. See? Everybody gone, come, came down here, you see? So all right. So what I did, I left. I went on and played with a band on this side of the river, up in, up in the Vashery. Here with a band, the Black Devil. Black Eagle, I mean what I'm saying? See? Played with them. See? I played there. Well after that, well I did, so I decided to come down here. See? So after I came down here, this boy here who was playing the band with me, El Concerto, see? Well he, his trumpeter died. See? So he sent for me to come down here in the Al Jays. How'd you know him?
I didn't know him, but he was-
He was sent for you, he worked for you?
Yeah, his brother-in-law.

His brother-in-law knows me because I come from Missouri, you see? He came from Missouri. So he told him, maybe you could get a fella I know to play trump with you. So there we sent him. But I was already down here with him. I lived on Cryo Street. See? So I got the letter and I came on him. Told me, you know, direct me just had to come, you know. I caught the ferry, Connelly Tree's ferry, came down. I walked all the way down from the ferry to the fire department there, you know? Walking up two blocks and then I turned, you see? So when I came, I came right straight to his house. Yeah, and his wife said, how you find this place? You see, you find this place better than us. I had no trouble, no. I had no trouble. So, all right. So after we, we all, we got the band together, you see? So we wouldn't do nothing but rehearsal. We rehearsal three or four times a week. We could get a lot of jobs, but we wouldn't take no job. So what, so what we done, we, uh, we, uh, just rehearsal. I think I did.
I closed the door.

Yeah, yeah, yeah. So, so he said, so we wouldn't, we wouldn't take no job. We just rehearsal. So after we, the first job we got, we played for some, oh, Beville Garden, on Beville Street. It rained all day and all night. And then the first job we played for White. That's in, uh, in the Algae area. In the Algae area, right in the Algae, up the Algae, right up the Algae area. Yeah, I know where they are. Yeah. So, all right. And we played, so after that, we, after we, we played there. Well, finally, well, we keep going, so finally, I say, well, I know the man, Moneta, you see? Yeah. From coming out there, my home. See, I never forgot him. And he came in and played in that pavilion, you know? He came in and played in that pavilion one night.
What was he?

With, uh, some band or nothing. I forgot the name of the band now. But he came there with that band and played. So, and I know him. So, I came down and sort of, I found that he was a teacher. So, well, I got me a book. And I went and took lessons from him. See? So, I took lessons there. I must have took lessons for two, three years, or something like that. And, uh... What kind of books, now?
We got to know everything.
Book? Wait, I'm going to show you the book.
You still got it? I'll show you the book. See? Charlie, DeGuard told me you studied hard. You should have a little man.

See this book there? This book just cost me three dollars. For that book. I didn't go all through that book, but I went through the first method, you see? Yeah. Uh-huh. I went halfway of that, you see?
You went halfway through Auburn's Complete Conservatory Method for Trumpet and Cornette. Yeah, yeah, yeah. Or so forth, so forth. Edited by Edwin Franco Goldman and Walter M. M as in mother, Smith.
Yeah. Yeah.
Newly Revised Authentic Edition. Uh-huh. And it's called Fisher Incorporated. Let's see if it's got a date on it. Copyright 1936. Uh-huh. So that's the Auburn method.
You've been halfway through that. Yeah, yeah. Three, that cost three dollars. Three dollars?
First got that for the head.
That's supposed to be the best area.
Yeah, uh-huh.
I'm the best.
Well, I know you don't want to give that away. So, no, I'll keep it.
So, uh-huh.
Yeah.

Well, after- after- after you see- you see the trouble is- all I had to do, like first over, see, all I had to do was learn the music. I already could play, you see. Yeah. You know the- you know- You could do the mouth thing.
Yeah, yeah.

Know the- you know the notes and then know the music. See, that's the only thing I had to learn, you know what I mean? Counting different songs and divides, you know what I mean? Right. So, well, after I got that down, so, you know, I feel good enough, you know what I mean, to- to read what I want to read. You know what I'm talking about? The music as much as I want, you see. So, well, we went on and so we continued playing, see. We just continued playing and we started- we played for mostly white. Most of the time we played for color, like in length. You see, in length, well, color used to give a lot. It had a fellow named Marrera. He used to always give really the team in length, all through length.
Who- who was that?
I don't know why. That's Red Crossy from the Moorover. We used to- or, uh, uh, man, I can't call that man name now.
Color saw had a- Italian.
Italian.
Italian saw gave dancers for color. Yeah, for color, yeah.

So, he, uh, we used to play all through length, you know, and then we used to play elsewhere, you know, for colors, you know. So, uh, played the Wool Forest Hall back at Gratner. The what? Wool Forest. Oh, the Wool Forest.
Yeah. The Wool's, the Wool's.
Yeah, I know the Wool's.
Yeah, for the Wool's.

Yeah, I used to play for them. We played picnic foam, you know, played dances foam and so on like that, you know. So, we, uh, we just keep it going, you know what I mean? The most, the most, the most, the most job we, we, we, we, we, you know, we do, most of the white, you see. Most white people. I played all down Lafitte. For Mr. Lillian. Down there, you know what I mean? Charlie Pozzin, played for him. All down there, you see. That's Lafitte. Lafitte. Played wrestling for Dutton LaBotte. Played down, uh, uh, Cutoff for Mr. Lee. Played, uh, down, uh, further down, uh, whatever that's at now. Yeah, played, we played on the Gulf of Mexico. What, on a boat? We used to go down on a boat. We used to go down on a boat. That's, that's the Grand Isles. Oh, Grand Isles? Yeah, Grand Isles. We played on a Grand Isles. We played on a Grand Isles. We played on a boat. We used to go down on a boat. We used to go down on a boat.
We used to go down on a boat. We used to go down on a boat.
We used to go down on a boat. That's, that's the Grand Isles. Oh, Grand Isles? Yeah, Grand Isles. We used to play down there. We was the first Cutoff man ever went, been on.
We used to go, had to go on a boat.

Every Saturday, we'd go on that boat. Every Saturday, man come get us and we go, we catch the boat in the feet. We go on the yacht. Man, that pretty boat, you see. We used to go down every Saturday. So finally, we had a fella bought a one of them boats from the governor. The submarine chaser, one of them boats was chased. Yeah, yeah. Well, they bought one of them and they used to charge two dollars a head. You know what I mean? Mostly all big time people, you know. The fellas used to like to gamble and things, so on like that, you know. So, well, we go down on that. So, but afterwards, well, we played for Mr. Sidney. We played for him. Definitely the Lee brothers and also Mr. Labatt and different people we played for. We sit all over and played. So many people now that we played for so long and forgot the name, you know what I mean? So, and then, well, we used to play all around the LJs, around the LJs, all over the river.
Lots of jobs going all the time.

Yeah, all over the river, you see. Then, we played at Fireman's Hall. When the first start giving dance was Jitney dance, you see. Jitney dance, I played that for eight or nine years there, you see. So, then by the Zalmo, I played there for Specs. That was Specs taught. Really?
Yeah.
I didn't know that. Yeah, we first, Specs taught giving dance, by the Zalmo, then, then he went to, uh, Shark Bay, they call it. That's a French. That's French.
Shark Bay.

Yeah, that down, that down the bar, you know. Yeah, Shark Bay, we played there in that place for him. And after that, after he left from there, he decided to run dance in Marrero, see, Walkerstown. See, that was a, that was a building, that was a building, it was nothing but a house, you know, a little grocery store, see. So, we started playing in there. For white?
Yeah, for white.
Me, Joe, me, Joe, and the boy, Buckeye, with the Buckeye. That's three pieces. What did he play?
He played saxophone.

Mm-hmm. So, we played, we played, uh, Joe James, man. Yeah, yeah, Joe James, too. On piano. Yeah, on piano. Yeah, on piano. But it's three, she was nothing but a house, like, you know, so, a room wouldn't, maybe we'll put this size, you know what I mean.

So, we'll find- Wait a minute, let's see how big is this place, man. They can't, they can't see the, the room on the tape, we better call them how big it is. How, how, how wide is this? A square room, about half, half, half on the side.
I'll be there, so, twelve by twelve, I'll be there, see.
He's playing in a place, twelve by twelve, with three pieces.
Yeah, three pieces.
You have more people in the band than the people there?

Yeah, sure. So, then look, then after that, you see, what he used to do, he used to give dancers one week for white. Then he reversed one week for color. See, alright. Why he used to do that? He want to see which, which raise he could make the moist money off, white or color. You see, so, alright. What he done, so he kept, he continued giving it, you see. So, well, Vinny's begin to build up. Want me to stop?
I'll stop it.
For white.
Pull him up, okay.

So, well, after that, well, he, the white, it looked like it was better for the white, see. So, what he did, he took down some of the petition in the place, you see. Uh-huh. Well, Vinny's begin to pick, really pick up good then, you see. Uh-huh. So, he said, well, I guess I need another, I need a dance hall now. So, this fella, the place was belongs for, he was Italian, you see. Well, he didn't have the money to build the dance hall, you see. So, the fella crossed the street, crossed the street, he have a military there, you see. So, he told the spectre, he said, well, if that fella want to build a dance hall for you, he said, I'll build it for you on the right hand side of the highway, on that side, you see. So, well, everyone, the fella decided, spectre got the money, and, uh, built the place, you see. So, after spectre built the place, we played there, we played for spectre, we opened the place and everything. So, after that, we left from spectre and we went back to Racelet, played for Dutton Lebar, you see. Played for him, went back there and played for the people out there. So, well, that made Elton, see, me and Elton was playing together. So, what we did, me and Joe got out of the band, see. See, he wanted to get rid of Joe, you see, fired Joe. Who did?
Elton Thedot, see.
Well, wait a minute.
When you went back to Racelet, you had Elton, Joe? No, no, I had Joe. Yeah.
Just the two of you? No, no, not two of us.
We just all had a new band, you see. Oh, well, how many people did that?
Edmund Warden, we had Edmund Warden. And, you had an Altar track? Yeah, Edmund Warden. I had a boy called Johnny Thomas, played drum. And had Albert playing trombone.
Albert Jackson.
No, he don't play anymore now.
What's he do now? Does he play anymore?
Albert Jackson. No, he don't play anymore now.
And he came to Lucci?

That's Lucci. That's his name. Lucci too. They called Lucci, but his right name is Albert. So well, we all played together. So, and after that, well, so Speck wanted us to come back again. So we came back again. And what happened? I tell you what happened. No, he, Speck, what they did Speck during time of the war, see? The fella want to buy this place out, see? And you see, after Speck, after this guy done paid Speck his money back when he put it in the building, you see? He double-crossed it. You see? He sold it place. The fella called Thomas C. Alright, so that made Speck was in the jam during time of the war. We had a lot of money on it then, you see? In the second edition. So, Speck did Speck, went all through the country buying used lumber to build that Moulin Rouge. See? Now we used to play in wrestling on Saturday. And we used to play Chapitula, La Pola and Chapitula, we used to play Wednesday, Friday, Wednesday and Friday. See? And Saturday we'd go to wrestling. And Sunday we'd come back and play on Chapitula Street, you see? That's for white a color on Chapitula? For white. That's white. Right on the corner.
What's the name of that place? I don't know.
I don't know the name of that. They had no house to go. What corner is it there? No, no. Right on the corner. Look. Right on the corner of Chapitula. On that side.
On the lake side?
Yeah, on that side, yeah. Going- Downtown Lake Corner.
Right hand side going back.
Yeah. Yeah.
Downtown Lake Corner.

Yeah. So, all right. So, well, all right. So, well, after that, after Speck had got this dance all completed, he wanted us to play at the Moulin Rouge for him, you see? We opened the Moulin Rouge. So he told Joey, he said, I'd like to get your band to play for me at the Moulin Rouge.
I said, Joey, sure? Yeah, sure.

So, well, what we did, we started playing for him. Well, we played all during the time of the war for him. See? And we, of course, in fact, we was the first ones starting out in dances. You see, he was a man who had a restaurant. He was in a restaurant up there by the Seller's Tax. You see, all up there didn't have nothing up at the Seller's Tax. No building at all around there. Nothing but used to raise garden and different things, you know. Just him and a fellow, a Italian fellow, he called Joe Bolina. You see, well, them only two fellows was there. So, well, every day, every day, well, they had a push wagon, you see? They put, make the sandwich, you know? Well, them days you could get a long sandwich there for a dime, you know?
How long is that?
Oh, a whole loaf of bread. For a dime. Like them days, everything was really cheap. Yeah, what you mean, 24 inches? Yeah, yeah. Or 36 inches? Yeah, a whole loaf. A whole loaf. Yeah.
How long is that, though? I don't know. About this loaf? I don't know. I don't know. About two feet, huh?
Yeah, I don't know how long loaf bread is, you know? Yeah. But you mean French bread, not light bread. Yeah, po'boy.
Po'boy loaf. Yeah. Yeah, yeah, you see? Yeah, well, they can't see that on the tape. He's just saying, well, I've got to get to this button.
Yeah, so he used to come every, you see, around about, say, between 10, 30, between 10, 30 and 11, something like that, you know?
Yeah. And they begin to come in the yard with the, with the sandwich and things, you see?

They come in the yard with the sandwich and, and, uh, about 12 o'clock below, well, they, they, uh, you know, everybody come to get a lunch, you know? Soft drink and so on like that, you know? Right. So, well, all right, Spick. So after that, he, he fooled around, I don't know, his wife, him and his wife had a little misunderstanding. So he separated. So he left him and went back to the country, you know, where she come from, the typical. So, uh, she sued him for most of all the money he had, you see? But he didn't have no money that broke him, you see? So that's how he come to start running dances.
Okay.

We first started running dances, you see? So, well, so after he started running dances, that's how he come to have the middle of the luge in the, in the, in the, in the, in the, in the road room, you see?
That's where you started drinking, huh?
Drinking?
Yeah.
No, no drinking.
Well, I hear you drink a fifth of whiskey every day.
Oh, I did. In the morning? Never drink. Never food liquor. For breakfast?
But for breakfast? Yeah.
For breakfast?
Yeah. No. You never had a drink in your lifetime? Yeah, I drink.

Yeah, I drink. I drink, you know, I take a little drink, I look, that's like a little beer. Now, I'm whatever I tell you. You know what I do? I have beer here, I drink maybe half of that beer and put the other half up. I don't even drink a whole bottle of salt drink. No?
Nuh-uh.
So, uh, uh, okay. You want to get it? Yeah, yeah, yeah. What do you call your wife? Call a babe.
Call a babe, huh? Uh-huh.
Yeah.
Babe call her, you know? Uh-huh.

That's nice. It's a nice name. Yeah. So, well, so I'll tell you, we've been fooling with Speck about, I've been fooling with Speck about 30 years almost. Uh-huh. See, so, uh, well, after we played for Speck all during the war, well, Benny's begin to drop off, you know? So, well, he quit giving dancing and he rented out, rented place out. So we start playing at the tip top. Yeah, he played the tip top. Played there. Played there a long time. Then I left, after we left from the tip top, we went, we go back, we go, I go back to the firewood hall, play for this fellow, but we wanted to find the firewood hall now. So, well, we played there, tell this guy, couldn't get along with him, so I quit the job, you see? So I quit the job, so I didn't like the way he carried on. So finally, well, now, after we left the firewood hall, we come back to the mall, you see? Played for this Anthony, Balala, you see? Anthony Balala. That's the fellow who got the place now, you see?
Got what, Speck's?

Yeah, he got the place now, you see? He built up new, you know, the remodeling place, built a new building now. Well, he's still going to have the place, you see, but he ain't going to have nothing but concrete allowance in there, you see? So Speck was expecting to manage that place again, but Speck didn't want to do him a partnership. He wanted, you know, just one man, you know what I mean? Because this fellow don't have a good reputation for business, you know? So, in fact, he don't run the place, no harm. He had the place, he chose, he rents it out, you see? You see, he rents cocktail lounge, three cocktail lounge, like if you want to lounge, if you want to lounge another phone, you rent it to you like that, you see? That's $150 a week, see?
So, alright, so Farah Lewell. $150, I didn't understand, $150 a week for how many? For one cocktail lounge or two or what? One.
$150 for one?
Yeah. And he's got three of them in there? Three. So he can make $450 a week out of that. Yeah, that's good money. If he gets the money.

That's over $600 a month. Yeah? Yeah. That's what he's doing alright. So, well, I tell you, well I really was sorry, you know what I mean? He didn't, you know, got that place, you know what I mean? See, because he'd be the honest man. But quite naturally, if anybody else would get it, they would do alright too, just the same. Except this fella here, you see? Because he, before, you see, when he had this cocktail lounge before, he had a different, a lot of cocktail lounge there where he had a lot of, you know, fast women, you know what I mean? See, no decent people.
Hostling? Yeah, yeah, yeah. Hostling women.
Yeah, yeah, no decent people would go, you know what I mean? That, you know what I mean?
So, and... Unless they want to get something decent.

Yeah, yeah, you see? So, well, so, well, after the place burnt down, the man burnt it down, the man that bought the place, I guess he burnt down, you know what I mean? It was going down in a hole, you know what I mean? So it's falling down, falling apart. So the man said, well, I guess the man must have set the fires up and get the insurance and get it done. It's really beautiful now, you know? They got a whole, the whole front is glass. And they already got a lot of doors. You can't, you ain't got no kick with getting out if something happened. You got a lot of doors, you know, back and forth. See? So, well, he finally didn't got the place. So, well, after that we left from there and then we started playing different places, you know, all over. Then I started playing over there for Larry, playing for him. See? You know, we used to play with, you know, maybe the-
Who was Larry? Larry, Bonstein.
Oh, Larry Bonstein.
Yeah, yeah.
You know? Yeah. See, we played, we started playing for him like maybe once a month, like, like they would have weddings or something like that we played, you know what I mean? Part of the season.
Yeah, yeah.
We played for him, you see? So, there it was. Then after, after that, well, we played different little jobs, different, you know, different places like that, you know. And, uh. Like what?

Like four different places. See, well. I can remember we went that night where they had all the artists and their statues and everything. Yeah. You got your picture in a book, you know? I played, I played.
You see that? Yeah, I played, yeah. With all those statues. You know, you're going, you come from England.
Do you sure? No, no. Not the banjo player. That's your boy that made that record of him, put it out in England. The banjo player. Yeah. That's your boy, isn't it?

Yes, that's him. The pirate. Yeah, yeah, yeah, yeah, yeah. He was living in that place. He was living there. In England? No, but he was living there when he was here. In that building one place of the part of the river.
Oh, yeah.
Yeah, he was living up in there. Cause that other, that, several people lived in there.
Oh, that was Mark Berger.

Yeah. The other one of them boys had a wife there too, you know what I mean? In that place, you know what I mean? So we played there for him. So then we played up to the school, you know, playing for the concert. Remember that concert we played?
Yeah, for Tommy Woods and Herbie Friedman. Yeah, for Herbie Friedman. We played for them.
Then after that we played several parts. We played for the ball game. The fellas of this boy had a ball club, you know? Oh, that was a fraternity. I think that was a K fraternity.
Yeah, yeah. We played for them out in the park.

See, we brought the piano and everything. And we played out there for them. So then we played, we played, we played, I played about three parties in the park. Yeah, the hillbilly got some good numbers. Really good ones. That's right, some really good numbers. I mean really- Oh, you play them well, man. Yeah, really, you know what I mean? Pepe, good numbers they got. You know what I'm talking about? The hillbilly. Now, they got rock and roll songs, they sound pretty good. I play some of them too. But the trouble is, when you play rock and roll songs, you got to have somebody sing it. Sing that number, you know what I mean? Somebody holler, you know? Not no singing, but holler. You see? You see, we had a boy playing, when we played at B-Wingwood, where he could sing rock and roll songs.
Who was that?
That's George James' nephew. Oh yeah, I remember him.
You remember him?

Well, you see, well, we used to play them numbers, people used to ask for them, what we, that's how we got him to sing with us, because he could sing them nothing, you see? It didn't pay you to just play it, it don't sound like nothing if you just played. You had to have somebody, you know, to holler. What are you doing, you ain't doing, but holler, you ain't singing, you know what I mean? So, well, we tried to satisfy the body, you know what I mean? So, sometimes, sometimes a fella come and sing, you know, like boy, white boy might come and say, acting set kid, I like to sing a little song, I know, I don't know if you know it. I said, yeah, well, go ahead. If we wouldn't know the song, we let him start singing first.
And pick it up.

And then we pick it up behind, you see? Sometimes, sometimes girls come and sing, you know what I mean? Different people would come, I want actors to sing, we let them sing, you know what I mean? Let them help their self, you know what I mean? I never, you know, they didn't mind it, you know what I mean?
Just like legends, they used to do that, they have to sing.

Yes, yes, some of them couldn't sing, no ha, you know what I mean? But I just, you know what I mean, just to keep them making hard feelings, you know what I mean? I let them sing, let them do what they could, you know what I mean? The best they could. So, well, well, you know, satisfied them, you know what I mean? Make them happy, you see? Make them happy, you see? Make them happy. So, they couldn't, they couldn't ever say, I was a fella who was disagreeable, you know what I mean? Just what they say, I was agreeable with them, you see? If right or wrong, it's all right with me, you know what I mean? So, sometimes, the couple of come up and said, that a girl used to always come, a lady used to come all the time. He'll be sad that she come. She come, you know, she be walking up, you know, I know she, she be coming up to the band then. I know what she want to do. And I'll ask her, I said, I said, well, I said, what you got new tonight? Oh, well, kid, I ain't got nothing to do with the same thing. The same song, you know what I mean? So, and, well, I let her sing it. So, there's another boy, Italian boy, he used to sing like, he used to sing like this fella, yeah. Oh, man, dead now. He used to blacken his face all the time. Al Jones. Al Jones. But you know what, dude, that fella could sing like that, don't you? He really could imitate him. But that boy's a good song, he can sing. He really could sing him. I didn't mind him sing, you know what I mean? And he sing different songs, you know what I mean? And I mean, sing just like that, that gal's one. That's right, I really sing. And so, he come, he sing, you know what I mean? Well, different people come and sing, you know. Sometimes we'll have like a company come, only bands, you know. Might have a few women's folks come there, you know. Maybe one of them can sing. Inspect was a fella, you know. Anybody would come around there, he think everybody come there could do something. You know, could play an ensemble, could do singing. Okay, he look, he didn't care if he could play a juicer, harmonica, anything. He want you to play some of that. He just love music, that's for- Yeah. Oh yeah, he loves music, you know what I mean? I know that. Sometimes he take his violin and play with us, you know. He could play pretty good, the violin, you know. And you know that guy that old man used to sit there playing sort of violin?
Oh, that's the cripple fella.

But you know him? Now you see, now a lot of people, you know a lot of people ask me about him? They thought he could play. No, he couldn't play nothing. Now that man, you know what I mean, that man been following us for years and years and years and years. Well, we go to that man and follow us. Uh huh. And uh, but he can't play nothing. But one thing, he know how to tune that violin. He can tune it. Oh yeah, he can. He really can tune that violin up in the right pitch, you know what I'm talking about? But just play anything, he couldn't play nothing. That's funny. And sometimes, man he be sewing on that violin and he be making a squeak, that little squeaky noise, boy it gets you kind of, you know what I mean, upset. That little noise going into your ear, you know. So, you know, we all have to stop him from that, that, that, on that violin, you know what I mean? So, sometimes a white boy come up there, you know, you know something white boy, you know, do a lot of mischievous things, you know. You know what they do sometimes, sometimes a white boy come down and put, rub grease on his string. See if he rub grease on that bow, you can't, you can't saw. See? See, you can't do nothing without you rubbing grease on that, you see. Sometimes come and take and rub that bow in the hair. And you see, if you have grease in your hair, you see, because now that grease get on there, you can't saw nothing, you know what I mean? But I used to feel sorry for him. I'd be Mr. If somebody broke this violin, I'd be Mr. Bill, get him a violin. Mr. Bill went over there and brought him a violin and gave it to him.

Thomas, you got time for one more? It's 435 now. For what? 435. 25 till 5. We better get up time, up the river? Yeah, we'll get up. Well, we'll call it to a halt then, because we just, this one's just about to run off. So we'll just let it run off then. Yeah, yeah, yeah. And we'll do it another time. Maybe you can come over by my house if you want to. Yeah, sure, yeah, sure. If you like, you see, and I can give you a gallon of whiskey. I think I'm over for breakfast, though.
Yeah, come over for breakfast. Mick, Mick, Mick, Mick.

segments.title: Opening: names and nicknames
segments.summary: Start of reel one; Valentine gives his name and nicknames and banter about middle names.

segments.title: Seeing Louis Armstrong twice in New Orleans
segments.summary: Asked about Louis Armstrong, he says he met him only after Armstrong came back, seeing him at the auditorium and the Gypsy Tea Room, around the war years.

segments.title: Teaching himself trumpet and the first three-number band
segments.summary: He had no method; he started on valve trombone, settled on trumpet and learned one number at a time until a small club band could play three numbers all night.

segments.title: First band members, the ballroom and the Niles band name
segments.summary: He names the first band's clarinet, banjo, bass and drum players, the ballroom and pavilion owned by brothers, and how a druggist named the band after his medicine.

segments.title: Band breaks up; playing with the Black Eagle band
segments.summary: The original players leave one by one, so he joins a band across the river, then is sent for to join a band in New Orleans.

segments.title: Arriving in New Orleans and rehearsing before taking jobs
segments.summary: He recalls the letter, the ferry and the walk to his new bandleader's house, and a band that only rehearsed for a long time.

segments.title: Lessons from Manuel Manetta
segments.summary: After first jobs he finds Moneta, a teacher he knew from home, and takes lessons for two or three years; he fetches his book.

segments.title: The Auburn conservatory trumpet method
segments.summary: The interviewer reads out the details of the trumpet method book; Valentine explains he already could play and only had to learn to read music.

segments.title: Playing dances for white and Italian-sponsored jobs along the river
segments.summary: He says most work was for white people, with some Italian-sponsored dances and halls for colored patrons.

segments.title: Jobs down Lafitte and Grand Isle boat gigs
segments.summary: A list of employers around Lafitte and Cutoff, and weekly boat trips to Grand Isle to play for gamblers.

segments.title: Playing Speck's dances: Jitney dances, Shark Bay and the twelve-by-twelve room
segments.summary: He plays jitney dances and then Speck's early dances in a tiny grocery in Marrero with a three-piece band, alternating white and colored nights.

segments.title: Speck builds a new dance hall; band changes
segments.summary: Speck builds a bigger hall, the band moves back and forth, Joe is fired, and a new line-up with Edmund Warden, Johnny Thomas and Albert Jackson forms.

segments.title: Building and opening the Moulin Rouge during the war
segments.summary: Speck buys lumber to build the Moulin Rouge; the band plays Chartres Street and wrestling-night dances, and opens the Moulin Rouge.

segments.title: How Speck came to run dances: sandwich seller turned promoter
segments.summary: He tells how Speck, once a restaurant man selling long loaves for a dime, lost his money in a divorce suit and started running dances.

segments.title: Drinking banter and his wife Babe
segments.summary: The interviewer teases about whiskey; Valentine says he only drinks a little beer, and they talk about his wife's nickname.

segments.title: After Speck: Tip Top, the firewood hall and the remodeled Moulin Rouge
segments.summary: After the war Speck quits, the band plays at various halls, and he discusses the new owner, the cocktail lounge rents and the burnt-down building.

segments.title: Playing for Larry Borenstein and odd jobs around town
segments.summary: He begins playing for Larry monthly and recalls jobs at an artists' party, a house with a banjo player, and others.

segments.title: School concerts, fraternity and law school parties, and a far-back dance hall
segments.summary: Concerts and parties for students and a dance in McDonoughville, then returning to Larry and the changes of ownership to Mills and Jaffe.

segments.title: Working for Mills and recording for him
segments.summary: Mills comes back from California, hires the band, nothing special happens, and they make recordings before returning to Jaffe.

segments.title: Missed Sammy, day jobs and painting
segments.summary: Talk about a Friday job, Sammy's packing work and his own work painting after being laid off from the railroad.

segments.chapter: Weddings and playing for private parties
segments.title: Herbie's wedding and the barefoot bride
segments.summary: He recalls a wedding he played, the bride's bare feet at a funeral parade, and the drummers and pianists who played.

segments.chapter: Weddings and playing for private parties
segments.title: Hunting for a pianist's name and a four-piece dance band
segments.summary: They try to recall a red-haired pianist and discuss a four-piece band in a big dance hall.

segments.title: Using the mute and dead versus live rooms
segments.summary: He explains that mutes suit loud rooms, not dead rooms like Preservation Hall, and how walls and no microphones change how hard he must blow.

segments.title: Dance tunes, waltzes and how dancing has changed
segments.summary: He says he plays slow and fast numbers to please everyone, complains modern dancers stay in the middle of the floor, and loves waltzes.

segments.title: Why his band plays different numbers than the other halls' bands
segments.summary: He compares Preservation Hall leaders with his own policy of always playing something different and learning new tunes on request.

segments.title: Bandmates over the years: Charlie Love, Henry Russ and a photograph
segments.summary: He names musicians who played with him, looks at a photograph with the interviewer and identifies bass and tenor players.

segments.title: Hillbilly numbers, rock and roll and the lack of new tunes
segments.summary: He says he bought hillbilly songs on request, claims rock and roll reuses old numbers, and dislikes rock and roll.

segments.title: Letting singers and guests sit in with the band
segments.summary: He needed a hollering singer for rock and roll numbers and let visitors, girls and an Al Jolson imitator sing.

segments.title: The man with the violin who followed the band
segments.summary: Valentine describes a man who followed the band and could tune a violin but not play, and the pranks done to him.

segments.title: Wrapping up the reel and an invitation to breakfast
segments.summary: The interviewer ends the session as the tape runs out and invites him over for another time.
